title: Supreme Court set to deliver ruling on Quebec's secularism law

image.caption: People watch the Supreme Court of Canada live broadcast in the lobby during hearings in March. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: What’s at stake as the Supreme Court rules on Quebec’s secularism law

The Supreme Court of Canada will make its decision on Quebec’s Bill 21 and could rule on the government’s pre-emptive use of the notwithstanding clause. The bill, enacted in 2019, bars some public workers in positions of authority from wearing religious symbols on the job. Friday’s ruling could also set new rules for how provinces across Canada can use the notwithstanding clause.

items: November 27Arguments for and against the bill — and what's at stake todayWhy all Canadians’ rights are at stake in the Supreme Court challenge of Quebec’s Bill 21Quebec’s Bill 21 bans religious symbols for some civil servants. Now, the legal battle has shifted from the ban itself to whether the province overstepped by invoking the notwithstanding clause in the text of the law, to bypass Charter rights.I covered the Supreme Court hearings of the Bill 21 case last spring for CBC Montreal, and I'll be covering the decision today. Let's talk a bit about what's at stake.First, there's the simple question of whether the ban on wearing religious symbols at work for some Quebec civil servants will be maintained or struck down. The overwhelming majority of people affected by Bill 21 and subsequent secularism laws are Muslim women who wear hijabs. Some teachers in Quebec have lost their jobs because of the ban, others have seen their careers stalled, and people studying to be teachers have abandoned that career path.But this case goes beyond the religious symbols ban. It's become much more about how the Quebec government used the constitutional notwithstanding clause to shield the ban from legal challenges.

How Bill 21 reached the Supreme CourtHolly CabreraPeople watch the Supreme Court of Canada live broadcast in the lobby during hearings in March. (Sean Kilpatrick/The Canadian Press)Today's ruling marks the latest chapter of a seven-year legal battle. In June 2019, the province's majority Coalition Avenir Québec (CAQ) government passed Bill 21, An Act Respecting the Laicity of the State, and pre-emptively invoked the notwithstanding clause — which is contained in the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms — to shield it from court challenges. The English Montreal School Board contested the law in Quebec Superior Court that October.In April 2021, Justice Marc-André Blanchard largely upheld the legislation, save for two exceptions: one for English-language school boards and another allowing National Assembly members to wear face coverings while sitting. The Quebec Court of Appeal overturned the exemption for English-language school boards in 2024, and the Supreme Court of Canada agreed to hear appeals in January 2025, setting the stage for today's decision.

Supreme Court to rule on Quebec's secularism lawHolly CabreraThe Supreme Court of Canada as seen from Parliament Hill in Ottawa. (Justin Tang/The Canadian Press)Canada's top court is getting ready to rule on Quebec's Bill 21, after spending months deliberating the province's secularism law.The case was heard over four days in March, making it one of the longest hearings in the history of the Supreme Court of Canada. A record 51 interveners took part in the proceedings, including six attorneys general. Bill 21 prevents employees in positions of authority in Quebec, such as teachers and police officers, from wearing religious symbols while on the job, and also requires civil servants to keep their faces uncovered when providing services. We'll bring you the decision as soon as the embargo lifts at 9:45 a.m. ET, along with the ensuing reaction and analysis.
